India is a country in South Asia. It is the seventh largest country by area and the most populous democracy in the world. India shares land borders with Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and Myanmar, and maritime borders with Sri Lanka and Indonesia.

The geography of India is extremely diverse, ranging from the snow-capped peaks of the Himalayas in the north to the tropical rainforests of the Western Ghats and the coastal plains of the eastern and western seaboards.

The Indian subcontinent rests on the Indian Plate, a minor tectonic plate within the Indo-Australian Plate. The northward movement of this plate against the Eurasian Plate created the Himalayan mountain range and the Tibetan Plateau over millions of years.

The Himalayas form the northern boundary of India and contain some of the highest peaks in the world, including Kanchenjunga and Nanda Devi. The range has three parallel belts: the Outer Himalayas, the Middle Himalayas, and the Greater Himalayas.

The Indo-Gangetic Plain lies south of the Himalayas and is one of the most fertile agricultural regions in the world. It is watered by the Indus, the Ganga, and the Brahmaputra river systems, which deposit alluvial soil across the plain.

The Thar Desert in northwestern India is a large arid region that experiences extreme temperatures. It receives very little rainfall and supports sparse vegetation and a pastoral economy.

The Deccan Plateau is a large tableland in southern India bounded by the Western Ghats on the west and the Eastern Ghats on the east. It is composed of ancient crystalline rocks and is drained by rivers such as the Godavari, the Krishna, and the Cauvery.

The Western Ghats are a mountain range running parallel to the western coast of India. They are older than the Himalayas and are recognized as a biodiversity hotspot, hosting a large number of endemic species of flora and fauna.

The Eastern Ghats are a discontinuous chain of hills along the eastern coast of India. They are lower and more eroded than the Western Ghats and are cut across by several major rivers.

India has a tropical monsoon climate for the most part. The southwest monsoon brings most of the annual rainfall between June and September, while the northeast monsoon affects the southeastern coast between October and December.

The southwest monsoon is driven by the seasonal reversal of winds over the Indian Ocean. It is influenced by the heating of the Tibetan Plateau, the position of the inter-tropical convergence zone, and phenomena such as El Nino and La Nina.

The northeast monsoon affects Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, and parts of Andhra Pradesh, contributing a significant share of their annual rainfall during the winter months.

Koppen's climate classification places most of India under the tropical wet and dry category, with variations including humid subtropical conditions in the north and arid conditions in the Thar.

India is drained by a large number of rivers, which are broadly divided into Himalayan rivers and peninsular rivers. Himalayan rivers such as the Ganga, the Indus, and the Brahmaputra are perennial and glacier-fed.

Peninsular rivers such as the Godavari, the Krishna, and the Mahanadi are largely rain-fed and show considerable seasonal variation in their flow. The Godavari is the longest river of peninsular India.

The Narmada and the Tapi flow westward into the Arabian Sea and drain through rift valleys, unlike the majority of peninsular rivers which flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal.

India's soils are classified into several broad categories including alluvial soil, black soil, red soil, laterite soil, and desert soil. Alluvial soil is found in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and is highly fertile.

Black soil, also known as regur, is found in the Deccan region and is well suited to the cultivation of cotton. It retains moisture well and develops deep cracks during the dry season.

Red soil is found in the southern and eastern parts of the peninsula. It is rich in iron and appears red due to the presence of iron oxide in the soil.

India's forests are classified into tropical evergreen forests, tropical deciduous forests, thorn forests, montane forests, and mangrove forests. The Sundarbans in West Bengal host the largest mangrove forest in the world.

Tropical deciduous forests, also known as monsoon forests, are the most widespread forest type in India. They shed their leaves during the dry season to conserve water.

The Sundarbans delta is shared between India and Bangladesh and is the habitat of the Royal Bengal Tiger. It is protected as a national park and tiger reserve.

India has a coastline of approximately 7,500 kilometres. The western coast includes the Konkan, the Malabar, and the Gujarat coast, while the eastern coast includes the Coromandel and the Northern Circars.

The Indian Ocean region is central to India's maritime security and economic interests. India's island territories include the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Lakshadweep archipelago in the Arabian Sea.

Natural hazards such as cyclones, floods, earthquakes, and droughts affect different parts of India with varying frequency and intensity. Cyclones typically strike the eastern coast during the pre-monsoon and post-monsoon seasons.

The National Disaster Management Authority coordinates disaster response across the country. It implements guidelines for preparedness, mitigation, and relief across all levels of government.

Earthquakes in India are concentrated in the Himalayan region, the northeastern states, and parts of Gujarat, reflecting the ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.

Urbanization in India has accelerated since independence, with cities such as Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, and Bengaluru emerging as major economic centres. Urban planning must contend with rapid population growth and infrastructure deficits.

Rural-urban migration is a persistent feature of the Indian economy, driven by the search for employment, education, and better public services. It contributes to the growth of slums and informal settlements in large cities.

Agriculture employs a large share of the Indian workforce and depends heavily on the monsoon. Irrigation projects, including dams and canals, have expanded agricultural output but have also raised concerns about groundwater depletion.

India's population is unevenly distributed, with high densities in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the coastal regions and lower densities in the Himalayas and the Thar Desert.

Population growth in India has slowed in recent decades due to rising literacy, urbanization, and the spread of family planning. The country is currently experiencing the demographic dividend as the working-age share of the population peaks.

Transport networks, including national highways, railways, ports, and airports, shape the geography of economic activity in India. The Golden Quadrilateral connects the four largest metropolitan centres.

Regional disparities in income, infrastructure, and human development remain a major challenge for Indian federalism. Special economic zones and industrial corridors aim to rebalance the spatial pattern of growth.

The climate of the Indo-Gangetic Plain is marked by very hot summers and cool winters, while the southern peninsula enjoys a more moderate temperature regime due to its proximity to the sea.

Altitude, latitude, and distance from the sea are the three principal controls of India's climate. The Himalayas act as a climatic barrier, shielding the subcontinent from cold continental air masses in winter.

India's river water disputes, such as the Cauvery and Krishna water disputes, illustrate the political geography of water sharing between states and the need for basin-level cooperation.

The concept of the demographic dividend refers to the economic growth potential that can result from shifts in a population's age structure, mainly when the share of working-age people is larger than the non-working-age share.

Climate change poses significant risks to India's coastlines through sea-level rise, stronger cyclones, and increased salinization of coastal aquifers. Coastal adaptation strategies include mangrove restoration and cyclone shelters.

The National Green Tribunal has jurisdiction over environmental cases and has played a role in regulating industrial pollution, deforestation, and the encroachment of wetlands.

River interlinking projects seek to transfer water from surplus basins to deficit basins to address regional water scarcity, although they raise ecological and inter-state concerns.

India's forest policy balances conservation with the rights of forest-dwelling communities. The Forest Rights Act recognizes the rights of traditional forest dwellers over land and resources.

The Central Water Commission advises the government on water resource planning and maintains data on river flows, reservoir levels, and irrigation potential across the country.

Glaciers in the Himalayan region are receding, threatening the long-term availability of water in glacier-fed rivers and increasing the risk of glacial lake outburst floods.

Groundwater meets about half of India's drinking and irrigation needs. Over-extraction has lowered water tables in many parts of the country, particularly in Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh.

India's monsoon rainfall exhibits considerable inter-annual variability. Drought years and flood years alternate, complicating agricultural planning and food security policy.

The Western Coastal Plain is narrower than the Eastern Coastal Plain and is bordered by the Western Ghats. It supports major ports such as Mumbai and Kochi.

The Eastern Coastal Plain is broader and more level, and is home to major deltaic regions formed by the Godavari, Krishna, and Cauvery rivers.

Ecosystem services provided by forests include carbon sequestration, watershed protection, soil conservation, and the provision of timber and non-timber forest products.

Biodiversity conservation in India is anchored in a network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, and biosphere reserves, supported by the Wildlife Protection Act.

India's location at the intersection of the Indian, Eurasian, and Burmese tectonic plates makes the northeastern region particularly prone to seismic activity.

The concept of sustainable development, as applied to Indian planning, requires balancing economic growth with environmental preservation and social equity across generations.

Natural vegetation in India varies with rainfall, temperature, and soil conditions, producing a rich mosaic of forest types from the wet evergreen forests of the northeast to the thorn scrub of Rajasthan.

The Coral Triangle and India's own reef ecosystems, such as the Gulf of Mannar and the Lakshadweep reefs, are biodiversity-rich but are threatened by bleaching and pollution.

The monsoon onset marks the start of the agricultural calendar in India. The timing and distribution of the monsoon determine sowing patterns and the success of the kharif crop.

The National Mission for Green India aims to increase forest cover and improve the quality of existing forests as part of India's commitments under the Paris Agreement.

Cyclonic disturbances in the Bay of Bengal are more frequent than those in the Arabian Sea, which is one reason why the eastern coast of India is more vulnerable to cyclones.

The groundwater crisis in India is compounded by the free or heavily subsidized supply of electricity for agricultural pumping, which encourages over-extraction of the resource.

India's western coast experiences heavier rainfall than the eastern coast because the Western Ghats intercept moisture-laden winds from the Arabian Sea.

The Peninsular Plateau is flanked by the Western Ghats on the west and the Eastern Ghats on the east, and its northern boundary is marked by the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.

River basins in India are the primary unit of water planning. The Ministry of Jal Shakti coordinates water resource development across state boundaries.

Desertification is a growing concern in arid and semi-arid parts of India, driven by overgrazing, deforestation, and unsustainable agricultural practices.

The Himalayas are still rising at a measurable rate due to continued convergence between the Indian and Eurasian plates, and this uplift is balanced by ongoing erosion.

Wetlands in India provide critical habitat for migratory birds and perform important functions of flood control and groundwater recharge. The Ramsar Convention lists several Indian wetlands of international importance.

The monsoons are the dominant feature of the Indian climate system, and the Indian Meteorological Department issues operational forecasts for their onset and progression.

Coastal regulation zones under the environmental law framework restrict construction and industrial activity within a defined distance of the high-tide line to protect fragile coastal ecosystems.

The north-east monsoon is also called the retreating monsoon, because it accompanies the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon and the southward shift of the ITCZ.

Soil erosion in the catchments of major rivers contributes to siltation of reservoirs and reduces their storage capacity and useful life.

The proportion of forest area to geographical area in India is about a quarter of the national territory, though the quality and density of forest cover vary widely between regions.

India is the third largest emitter of greenhouse gases in the world, and its energy transition toward renewables is central to global climate negotiations.

The Himalayan watershed supplies major perennial rivers that support the Indo-Gangetic Plain, one of the most densely populated agricultural regions on Earth.

Water storage per capita in India is among the lowest in the world, which heightens the importance of groundwater recharge and demand-side management.

Mangrove ecosystems along the Indian coast act as natural storm barriers and nursery grounds for fisheries, making their conservation a coastal defense priority.

The term monsoon is derived from the Arabic word mausim, meaning season, and refers to the seasonal reversal of winds and associated rainfall over the Indian subcontinent.

Urban heat islands raise temperatures in large Indian cities relative to their rural surroundings, compounding the health impacts of heat waves.

India's economic geography is shifting with the rise of information technology hubs in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune, which attract skilled labour from across the country.

The planning of national highways follows the North-South and East-West corridor scheme, supplementing the Golden Quadrilateral network.

Fisheries along the Indian coast contribute significantly to livelihoods and nutrition, and are managed through marine fisheries regulation across exclusive economic zones.

India's eastern boundary includes the Indo-Myanmar border, and the northeastern states are linked to the rest of the country through the narrow Siliguri corridor.

The Sundarbans are repeatedly affected by cyclones, storm surges, and sea-level rise, threatening both the tiger population and the human settlements in the region.

The carrying capacity of India's river basins is increasingly stressed by population growth, urbanization, and industrial water demand.

Drought-prone areas of India include parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, and the Deccan interior, where rainfall is low and erratic.

India's islands, both in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, have strategic importance for maritime surveillance and for the projection of naval power.

The kharif cropping season coincides with the southwest monsoon, while the rabi season is cultivated in the drier post-monsoon winter months using irrigation.

Renewable energy from solar parks in Rajasthan, wind farms in Tamil Nadu, and hydroelectric projects in the Himalayas is reshaping India's energy geography.

The concept of river rejuvenation refers to the restoration of the ecological health of rivers through pollution abatement, flow restoration, and wetland conservation.

India's national water policy emphasizes integrated water resource management and the treatment of water as an economic as well as a social good.
